cues.text: Welcome to Chemical Kinetics.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Kinetics asks how quickly a reaction proceeds.
Equilibrium asks about its preferred composition.
A thermodynamically favourable reaction can still be slow.
Average rate describes a finite interval; instantaneous rate is the local
slope
of the concentration time curve.
For two A forming B at constant volume, A disappears twice as quickly as B
forms.
Divide the disappearance rate of A by its coefficient two to obtain the
normalized reaction rate.
If A disappears at zero point zero four zero molar per second, the reaction
rate is zero point zero two zero molar per second.
Read whether the question asks for a species rate or the normalized rate.
Now determine a rate law from experiments.
Our first experiment uses A and B concentrations each zero point one zero
molar
and gives rate zero point zero zero two zero molar per second.
In the second, only A doubles and the rate quadruples.
The exponent of A is therefore two.
In the third, only B doubles and the rate doubles.
Its exponent is one.
The law is k times A squared times B, with total order three.
Do not copy those exponents from an overall chemical equation; they are
experimental results.
Substitute the first row to find k.
Divide zero point zero zero two zero by zero point one squared times zero
point
one.
The result is two point zero, with units molar to the minus two per second.
At unchanged temperature and conditions, tripling A and halving B changes rate
by nine times one half, or four point five.
Each concentration ratio gets its own exponent.
Overall order three does not mean every mixed change gets cubed.
Order and molecularity answer different questions.
Total order is the sum of exponents in an empirical rate law.
It may be zero or fractional.
Molecularity counts reacting entities in a single elementary step and is a
positive integer.
Do not assign molecularity to an arbitrary multistep overall equation.
If rate uses concentration per time and total order is r, the units of k are
concentration to the power one minus r, divided by time.
A first order k has inverse time units.
A zero order k has concentration per time units.
For an order of one half, k has concentration to the one half per time.
Units are a useful check, not a substitute for reading the experiment.
For zero order disappearance, the concentration decreases by a fixed amount
per
unit time while the model holds.
Integrating gives concentration at time t equals initial concentration minus k
times t.
A plot of concentration against time is straight with slope minus k.
Take initial concentration zero point zero eight zero zero molar and k zero
point zero zero two zero zero molar per minute.
After fifteen minutes the loss is zero point zero three zero zero molar,
leaving zero point zero five zero zero.
Setting concentration to zero gives depletion time forty minutes.
Extrapolating beyond that would predict a negative concentration and is
physically invalid.
The zero order half life is initial concentration divided by two k.
Here it is twenty minutes.
Doubling the initial concentration doubles that half life at the same k.
A zero order description can apply over a limited range, such as a saturated
catalyst surface.
State its valid range rather than assuming that the same straight line governs
every possible concentration.
For first order disappearance, the rate is proportional to the amount still
present.
Equal time intervals remove equal fractions rather than equal amounts.
The integrated law is the natural logarithm of initial concentration divided
by
remaining concentration equals k times t.
The ratio inside the logarithm is dimensionless.
The half life is natural log two divided by k and is independent of the
starting concentration in this model.
Suppose the half life is ten minutes.
Thirty minutes is three half lives, so the fraction remaining is one half
cubed, or one eighth.
That is twelve point five percent remaining, not twelve point five percent
consumed.
For ninety percent completion, ten percent remains.
Calculate k as natural log two divided by ten, about zero point zero six nine
three one per minute.
The required time is natural log ten divided by k, about thirty three point
two
minutes.
Never replace percent remaining by percent consumed inside the logarithm.
Here is another check.
A reactant is seventy five percent consumed in twenty minutes.
One quarter remains, so two half lives have elapsed and each half life is ten
minutes.
To reach ninety three point seven five percent consumption, one sixteenth must
remain.
That is four half lives in total, or forty minutes.
The additional time after the first observation is twenty minutes.
A plot of natural log concentration against time is straight with slope minus
k, using a consistent concentration reference.
Finally, keep the time unit consistent.
A k value of zero point one two zero per minute equals zero point zero zero
two
zero zero per second.
Multiplying an inverse minute constant by a time in seconds without conversion
gives the wrong decay.
Pressure measurements can reveal a rate constant, but only after stoichiometry
connects pressure to the reactant.
Assume initially pure ideal gas A decomposes to one B plus one C.
Temperature and volume stay constant, and no other gases or reactions are
present.
Let the reacted fraction be f.
Starting with n zero moles, the remaining A is n zero times one minus f.
The amounts of B and C are each n zero f.
Total moles are therefore n zero times one plus f.
At fixed temperature and volume, total pressure divided by initial pressure
equals one plus f.
If the initial pressure is one hundred kilopascals and the total pressure
after
ten minutes is one hundred fifty, f is one half.
Remaining A has partial pressure fifty kilopascals.
Equivalently, A's partial pressure is twice the initial pressure minus the
current total pressure.
Use that partial pressure in the first order disappearance law, because it is
proportional to A concentration under the stated conditions.
k equals natural log of one hundred divided by fifty, all divided by ten
minutes.
The answer is about zero point zero six nine three per minute.
Total pressure rises because one reactant molecule produces two product
molecules, while the amount of A falls.
Directly inserting total pressure into a disappearance formula would give the
wrong sign.
Check the limiting pressures.
At the beginning, total pressure is one hundred.
At complete conversion it approaches two hundred in this model.
If the reaction stoichiometry, initial mixture, temperature or volume changes,
derive a new pressure relation.
Do not memorize twice initial minus total as a universal gas kinetics formula.
The reliable method is a mole balance followed by the ideal gas relation.
The Arrhenius model writes k as A times the exponential of minus activation
energy divided by R T.
Use temperature in kelvin and match the energy units of activation energy and
R.
If A is approximately constant and activation energy is positive, higher
temperature increases k.
Comparing two temperatures gives natural log of k two over k one equals
activation energy over R, multiplied by one over T one minus one over T two.
Suppose k doubles between three hundred and three hundred ten kelvin.
Use R equal to eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin.
Activation energy is R times natural log two, divided by one over three
hundred
minus one over three hundred ten.
The result is about fifty three thousand six hundred joules per mole, or fifty
three point six kilojoules per mole.
The sign is positive, as expected.
A plot of natural log k against inverse temperature has slope minus activation
energy over R.
There is no universal rule that every ten degree rise doubles every reaction
rate.
In elementary collision theory for gaseous bimolecular reactions, encounters
need sufficient energy and suitable orientation.
Counting all collisions as successful would overestimate the reaction rate.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower effective activation
barrier and speeds the approach to equilibrium.
At unchanged temperature it does not change the equilibrium constant or the
reaction enthalpy.
It may participate in intermediate steps without being consumed in the net
reaction.
Finish each kinetics problem by identifying the rate definition, selecting the
order and model, converting units, and checking physical limits.
Use the twelve original practice questions and the seven worked examples in
the notes.
This recording covers the core foundation of Unit eight; broader experimental
datasets and mechanism practice remain useful.
The questions are original practice, not official past papers.
A reaction rate and a species disappearance rate are not always the same
number.
For the balanced decomposition of two moles of dinitrogen pentoxide into four
moles of nitrogen dioxide and one mole of oxygen, divide each concentration
slope by its stoichiometric coefficient.
Suppose dinitrogen pentoxide disappears at zero point zero zero four zero
moles
per litre per second at constant volume.
The normalized forward reaction rate is half that value, zero point zero zero
two zero.
Nitrogen dioxide appears four times as fast as the normalized rate, giving
zero
point zero zero eight zero.
Oxygen appears at zero point zero zero two zero.
All three statements describe the same reaction progress.
The negative sign in a disappearance derivative makes the forward rate
positive; it does not mean the concentration is negative.
These coefficient relationships follow from stoichiometry, while experimental
concentration exponents in a rate law are a different matter.
If volume changes substantially, account for that change before identifying a
concentration derivative with a simple molar production rate.
Read exactly which species and which definition the question requests.
A reaction can appear first order when one concentration remains nearly
constant.
Consider an experimentally established disappearance law for A equal to k
times
A concentration times B concentration.
If B is present in very large excess, consuming A changes B only slightly
over the measurement interval.
Combine k and the effectively constant B concentration into an observed first
order constant.
With k equal to zero point zero two zero litres per mole per second and B
concentration zero point five zero moles per litre, the observed constant is
zero point zero one zero per second.
The predicted half life of A is about sixty nine point three seconds.
The original constant still has second order units, while the observed
constant
has inverse time units.
Doubling the maintained B concentration doubles the observed constant and
halves that half life within the model.
This does not turn the underlying overall order into a universal first order
law.
If B is depleted significantly, the approximation fails.
In ester hydrolysis examples, solvent and catalyst conditions must also be
controlled rather than silently absorbed into an unexplained constant.
Graph selection can distinguish an amount removed from a fraction removed.
Under zero order disappearance, concentration itself decreases linearly with
time and the slope is minus the zero order constant.
For first order disappearance, the natural logarithm of the remaining
concentration divided by its initial value is linear, with slope minus the
first order constant.
Using the ratio keeps the logarithm dimensionless.
Equal successive half lives support a first order model; a half life
proportional to starting concentration supports zero order over its applicable
range.
Suppose a first order logarithmic plot has slope minus zero point zero three
zero per minute.
The constant is positive zero point zero three zero per minute and half life
is
about twenty three point one minutes.
A straight concentration plot with slope minus zero point zero zero three zero
moles per litre per minute instead has a zero order constant with
concentration
per time units.
Do not compare those numerical slopes as if their units matched.
A good fit over a narrow interval is evidence for a model, not proof of an
elementary mechanism.
A completion percentage must be converted into the fraction still present.
For a first order reactant with a ten minute half life, seventy five percent
completion leaves one quarter, requiring two half lives or twenty minutes.
Eighty seven point five percent completion leaves one eighth, requiring thirty
minutes.
Ninety nine point nine percent completion leaves one thousandth, not nine
hundred ninety nine thousandths.
Its time is the natural logarithm of one thousand divided by the constant.
Since the constant is the natural logarithm of two divided by ten minutes, the
time is about ninety nine point seven minutes.
Thus nearly ten half lives are needed, even though the final amount is very
small.
Exact one hundred percent completion would require the logarithm of an
infinite
concentration ratio in this ideal continuous model; it has no finite predicted
time.
Real measurements have detection limits and the model may cease to apply at
very low concentrations.
For the same first order law, the ratio of ninety percent completion time to
half life is the natural logarithm of ten divided by the natural logarithm of
two.
An energy profile separates a barrier from the energy difference between
products and reactants.
In an illustrative single barrier enthalpy diagram, set reactants at zero and
products at minus thirty kilojoules per mole.
An uncatalysed peak at plus eighty gives a forward barrier of eighty and a
reverse barrier of one hundred ten.
The reverse barrier is measured upward from the lower product level, not from
zero.
If an alternative catalytic path has a peak at plus sixty with the same
endpoints, its forward and reverse barriers are sixty and ninety.
Both decrease, while the reaction enthalpy remains minus thirty.
A real catalytic mechanism can contain several intermediates and barriers;
this
simple diagram illustrates the bookkeeping.
The catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature,
although it can change how quickly equilibrium is approached.
Barrier differences alone do not guarantee a numerical rate ratio unless the
relevant prefactors and kinetic model are also specified.
Keep potential energy sketches, thermodynamic direction and experimentally
measured rates distinct.
An Arrhenius graph is useful only after identifying both axes and the
logarithm
convention.
For a fixed mechanism with an approximately constant pre exponential factor,
the natural logarithm of the rate constant equals the natural logarithm of
that
factor minus activation energy divided by R T.
A graph of natural logarithm k against reciprocal absolute temperature
therefore has slope minus activation energy divided by R.
Suppose its measured slope is minus six thousand kelvin.
Multiplying the positive magnitude by R, eight point three one four joules per
mole kelvin, gives activation energy forty nine point eight eight four
kilojoules per mole.
If the vertical axis instead uses base ten logarithm k, the slope contains an
additional factor two point three zero three in the denominator.
Applying the natural logarithm formula to that graph would give the wrong
energy.
Also inspect horizontal scaling: a graph against one thousand divided by
temperature does not have the same numerical slope as one against reciprocal
temperature.
A straight segment supports a useful model over its measured range; it does
not
prove the mechanism and pre exponential factor remain unchanged at every
temperature.
Experimental reaction order need not be an integer and need not equal a
balanced equation coefficient.
Consider three initial rate measurements at the same temperature and with the
same preparation conditions.
In the first experiment, A and B concentrations are both zero point one zero
zero molar, and the initial rate is zero point zero zero two zero molar per
second.
In the second, A is increased fourfold while B stays fixed, and the rate
doubles.
Thus four raised to the order in A equals two, giving order one half.
In the third experiment, return A to its original value and triple B.
If the initial rate triples, the order in B is one.
The overall order is three halves.
Dividing rate by the square root of A concentration and by B concentration
gives a rate constant with units molarity to the negative one half per second.
Fractional order describes an observed rate law; molecularity is a count for
an
elementary event and is not assigned a fractional value.
Use initial rates so changing composition during a run does not obscure the
controlled comparison.
A sudden concentration decrease is not always evidence that reactant has been
consumed.
Take a first order reaction in a closed well mixed liquid, with rate constant
zero point zero six nine three one per minute.
At the selected instant there are zero point one zero zero moles of reactant
in
one litre.
Add inert solvent rapidly so the volume becomes two litres, with no reaction
during the idealized mixing step.
The amount remains zero point one zero zero moles, but concentration falls
from
zero point one zero zero to zero point zero five zero zero molar.
After mixing, assume the temperature, medium effects and first order rate
constant remain unchanged.
Ten minutes later, about half the amount remains: zero point zero five zero
zero moles in two litres, or zero point zero two five zero zero molar.
Using the original concentration as though no dilution occurred would mistake
mixing for additional reaction.
Real dilution may alter a rate constant through solvent or ionic effects;
constancy is an assumption here.
Keep separate records of amount, volume and elapsed reaction time before
choosing an integrated concentration ratio.
As a supporting rate law application, suppose one reactant can form either B
or
C through independent irreversible first order pathways.
Let the rate constants be zero point zero two zero and zero point zero three
zero per minute, respectively.
Assume both stay constant, the products do not react further, and the initial
products are absent.
Reactant disappears through both channels, so its total first order loss
constant is zero point zero five zero per minute.
Its half life is the natural logarithm of two divided by that total, about
thirteen point eight six minutes.
Product formation rates have ratio two to three at every instant, because both
contain the same current reactant concentration.
Integrating gives forty percent of reacted A as B and sixty percent as C in
this ideal model.
When half of an initial one mole has reacted, B amount is zero point two zero
mole and C amount zero point three zero mole.
These are fractions of reacted material, not fractions of the remaining
reactant.
Reversible steps, product loss or different orders require another model;
adding constants blindly is not a general rule for reaction networks.
A measured signal can track concentration without being equal to
concentration.
Suppose a first order disappearance is monitored by a calibrated signal S
equal
to a constant baseline plus a constant factor times reactant concentration.
The baseline is zero point one zero zero, the initial signal zero point nine
zero zero, and the signal after ten minutes zero point five zero zero.
Subtracting the baseline gives an initial excess zero point eight zero zero
and
a later excess zero point four zero zero.
The concentration fraction remaining is one half, so the rate constant is
natural logarithm two divided by ten, or zero point zero six nine three one
per
minute.
Using the raw ratio zero point five divided by zero point nine would be
incorrect.
This analysis assumes a linear calibration, a constant response factor and an
endpoint signal that represents complete reactant disappearance.
Other absorbing species or instrumental drift require their own model.
A fitted first order constant describes the observed kinetic law, not
necessarily an elementary step.
A reaction experiencing two temperature stages cannot generally use a simple
arithmetic average of rate constants.
Consider a first order disappearance in a fixed volume with no material added
or removed.
During the first ten minutes, the supplied rate constant is natural logarithm
two divided by ten per minute.
Half of the initial reactant remains.
During the next five minutes at a different temperature, the rate constant is
natural logarithm two divided by five per minute.
This stage removes half of what remains, leaving one quarter of the initial
amount overall.
Each segment contributes its own dimensionless exposure, k times time.
The total exposure is two natural logarithms of two.
An effective constant for the whole fifteen minutes is this sum divided by
fifteen, about zero point zero nine two four two per minute.
It is a time weighted summary for this schedule, not the rate constant at an
average temperature.
This model treats temperature changes as instantaneous and ignores conversion
during the transitions.
Finite heating ramps instead require an integral of the temperature dependent
constant over time.
Comparing activation energies alone is insufficient when Arrhenius prefactors
differ.
Use two supplied first order processes at three hundred kelvin.
Process X has a prefactor one tenth that of process Y, while its activation
energy is lower by R T times natural logarithm ten at this temperature.
The energy advantage is about five point seven four kilojoules per mole using
R
equal to eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin.
In the ratio of Arrhenius constants, the prefactor contributes zero point one
and the exponential contributes ten.
Their product is one, so the two rate constants are equal at three hundred
kelvin.
This equality need not hold at another temperature if the activation energies
and prefactors remain fixed.
A prefactor has the units of its own rate constant; numerical comparisons
require compatible rate law definitions and units.
The example does not infer an elementary mechanism or a universal compensation
rule.
Separate the energy dependent exponential from collision frequency and
orientation contributions before turning a barrier comparison into a numerical
rate prediction.
A sequential reaction can make an intermediate accumulate and then disappear.
This is a supporting application of first order laws, not an additional
required integrated order formula.
Consider the ideal sequence A forming B, followed by B forming C, with both
irreversible steps having the same constant k in a fixed volume.
Initially only A is present, and each step has one to one stoichiometry.
Use the supplied result: the fraction present as B is k t times exponential
minus k t.
At time one divided by k, that fraction reaches its maximum, one divided by e,
about zero point three six eight.
At that instant A also has fraction one divided by e, and C has fraction one
minus two divided by e, about zero point two six four.
The three fractions sum to one.
If k is zero point one zero zero per minute, the intermediate peaks at ten
minutes.
Unequal rate constants, reverse reactions or material removal change these
expressions.
A falling intermediate concentration does not mean its formation has stopped;
it means its consumption rate exceeds its formation rate.
A clock measurement records the time needed to reach a specified chemical
threshold.
It does not directly measure a rate constant.
Suppose a calibrated iodine clock signals after a cumulative iodine production
of zero point zero zero zero two zero zero mole per litre of final mixture.
This is iodine produced over the interval, not necessarily free iodine
accumulated, because a fast auxiliary reaction can consume iodine until its
scavenger is exhausted.
Reaching that same threshold in twenty seconds gives average iodine formation
rate one point zero zero times ten to the negative five mole per litre per
second.
Forty seconds gives half that rate.
Comparing reciprocal times is valid only when the threshold and volume
convention match.
If conversion is small enough that reactant concentrations barely change,
these
averages may approximate initial rates.
A large threshold, changing scavenger amount, mixing delay or a different
detection criterion can invalidate that shortcut.
In the thiosulfate clock model, two thiosulfates consume one iodine, so the
cumulative iodine threshold is half the initial thiosulfate concentration in
the final mixture.
This is interpretation of supplied measurements, not a preparation procedure.
Average and instantaneous rates answer different questions about the same
concentration curve.
Consider a supplied first order disappearance at fixed volume with initial
concentration zero point one zero zero molar and rate constant zero point one
zero zero per minute.
After ten minutes, concentration is zero point one times exponential minus
one,
about zero point zero three six eight molar.
The mean disappearance rate over those ten minutes is the lost concentration
divided by ten, about zero point zero zero six three two molar per minute.
At the midpoint, five minutes, the instantaneous rate is instead k times the
concentration at that instant, about zero point zero zero six zero seven molar
per minute.
A secant slope over an interval and a tangent slope at one time need not
agree,
even if that time is the interval midpoint.
For this decaying exponential the rate falls continuously as reactant
disappears.
Shortening an interval around a chosen instant makes its mean approach the
tangent value, subject to measurement uncertainty.
A straight line concentration trace would be a different case in which
interval
and tangent slopes are equal.
Concentration can fall because a substance reacts and because its occupied
volume increases.
As a supporting material balance, consider a uniform closed reacting system
whose boundary can move, with no inflow or outflow of A.
Write its amount as concentration times volume.
Differentiating that product gives amount change equal to volume times
concentration change plus concentration times volume change.
Define the positive chemical disappearance rate per current volume as r.
Then the concentration derivative is negative r minus concentration divided by
volume times the volume derivative.
At a specified instant let volume be one litre, A concentration zero point one
zero zero molar, chemical disappearance rate zero point zero zero two zero
zero
molar per second and expansion rate zero point zero one zero zero litre per
second.
The expansion contributes an additional concentration decrease of zero point
zero zero one zero zero molar per second.
The observed concentration slope is therefore negative zero point zero zero
three zero zero, while chemical amount loss is only zero point zero zero two
zero zero mole per second.
This distinction extends the constant volume rate definition; it is not an
additional required integrated order law.
A reversible first order model approaches an equilibrium plateau rather than
consuming all reactant.
Consider a fixed volume closed system with one to one conversion between A and
B.
Let forward and reverse constants be zero point one zero zero and zero point
zero five zero zero per minute, and let their conserved total concentration be
zero point three zero zero molar.
Equal opposing rates at equilibrium give B to A concentration ratio two.
The equilibrium concentrations are therefore zero point two zero zero molar B
and zero point one zero zero molar A.
The supplied relaxation result says displacement from equilibrium decays with
the sum of the two constants, zero point one five zero per minute.
Its half time is natural logarithm two divided by that sum, about four point
six two minutes.
Starting with only A, after one such half time B is zero point one zero zero
molar and A is zero point two zero zero.
This halves the distance to equilibrium, not the initial A concentration.
It is a supporting kinetic model, not a universal formula for every reversible
mechanism.
The ratio of these two constants describes equilibrium only for the stated
compatible rate laws.
The statement that a reaction doubles its rate constant for every ten degree
rise is an approximate shortcut, not a universal Arrhenius identity.
Suppose the rate constant doubles between three hundred and three hundred ten
kelvin.
Assume one unchanged mechanism, a temperature independent activation energy
and
a constant pre exponential factor across the small range.
The logarithm of the rate constant ratio equals activation energy over the gas
constant times the difference of reciprocal absolute temperatures.
Using the gas constant eight point three one four gives an activation energy
about fifty three point six kilojoules per mole.
For the next interval, three hundred ten to three hundred twenty kelvin, the
reciprocal temperature difference is smaller.
Divide that new difference by the first difference to obtain three hundred
over
three hundred twenty.
The next multiplier is therefore two raised to that ratio, approximately one
point nine one five, rather than exactly two.
This calculation compares rate constants.
Actual reaction rates also depend on concentrations through the experimental
rate law.
Use kelvin throughout, preserve the sign, and do not extrapolate a fitted
activation energy across a mechanism change.
A total pressure measurement contains every gas, including an inert gas that
does not react.
Consider a closed rigid vessel at constant temperature.
Initially reactant A has partial pressure eighty kilopascals and an inert gas
has forty kilopascals.
There is initially no product.
The only reaction is one A forming two B.
Let the pressure equivalent of the reacted amount be x.
Reactant pressure becomes eighty minus x, product pressure becomes twice x,
and
inert pressure stays forty.
Total pressure is therefore one hundred twenty plus x.
At a measured total pressure of one hundred sixty kilopascals, x is forty,
leaving reactant pressure forty and product pressure eighty.
If disappearance is first order and this reading occurs after one hundred
seconds, the rate constant is the natural logarithm of two divided by one
hundred, about zero point zero zero six nine three per second.
The correct reconstruction uses twice the initial reactant partial pressure
plus inert pressure minus total pressure.
Twice the initial total pressure minus the current total pressure would give
the wrong result.
These equations require ideal gases, fixed temperature and volume, and the
supplied single reaction.
A calculated rate constant inherits the uncertainty of the measurement used to
obtain it.
Consider a supporting inference exercise under an already accepted
irreversible
first order model, at fixed temperature and volume.
After one hundred seconds, a calibrated experiment bounds the fraction
remaining between zero point four eight and zero point five two.
Treat these as supplied bounds, not as a statistical confidence interval, and
neglect timing error.
The rate constant equals negative natural logarithm of the fraction divided by
time.
Because the logarithm increases with its argument, the larger remaining
fraction gives the smaller disappearance constant.
The lower constant is negative logarithm of zero point five two divided by one
hundred, about zero point zero zero six five three nine per second.
The upper constant uses zero point four eight, about zero point zero zero
seven
three four zero per second.
Half life is natural logarithm of two divided by the constant, so its bounds
run in the opposite order: approximately ninety four point four to one hundred
six seconds.
A midpoint measurement would suggest one hundred seconds, but cannot erase the
supplied interval.
One bounded reading also does not establish the reaction order by itself.
A proposed mechanism can contain species absent from the net reaction, yet
those species can affect its rate.
Use a hypothetical supporting mechanism with a fast reversible association of
A
and B to form intermediate I, followed by a slow elementary reaction of I with
C to give P and regenerate B.
Adding the forward steps cancels I and B, leaving A plus C forming P.
Intermediate I is produced first and consumed later.
Catalyst B is consumed first and regenerated later.
If the fast first step remains close to equilibrium while the slow step
consumes I, its concentration is the concentration equilibrium constant times
free A times free B.
The slow elementary step has rate constant k two times I times C.
Substitution gives k two times the equilibrium constant times free A, free B
and C: an apparent third order law in this specified regime.
The two elementary forward steps are each bimolecular; there is no three body
elementary collision implied by the overall third order law.
Free B must not automatically be replaced by total catalyst when appreciable B
is bound in I.
This conditional derivation illustrates reasoning, not proof that a real
reaction follows this mechanism.
An experimental rate law is a claim about independently controlled variables,
not just a pattern in one table.
Suppose the law is rate equals k times concentration A to power m times
concentration B to power n.
A first comparison doubles both concentrations and gives a fourfold rate.
This fixes the sum of the two orders at two, but it does not establish that
each order is one.
Orders two and zero, one and one, or zero and two all satisfy that comparison.
Now use an additional experiment that doubles A alone while keeping B and
temperature fixed.
If this also gives a fourfold rate, the order in A is two.
Combining that result with the earlier sum gives order zero in B over the
tested range.
The zero order is an empirical local statement, not proof that B never
participates in any molecular step.
Uncontrolled temperature, dilution or catalyst changes would compromise the
inference.
Design the extra comparison to break the ambiguity instead of reading balanced
equation coefficients as measured exponents.
Collision theory separates encounter frequency from the chance that an
encounter produces a reaction.
In a selected elementary gas collision model, stipulate that two percent of
collisions satisfy the chosen energy criterion.
Among those energetic collisions, only one tenth have a suitable relative
orientation.
The fraction satisfying both requirements is two percent times one tenth,
which
is zero point two percent of all collisions.
If the system has a supplied total collision count of one million per second,
this ideal comparison predicts two thousand successful events per second.
That event count is not automatically a molar rate constant; converting
between
event counts and concentration based rates requires the appropriate amount,
volume and pair count conventions.
Increasing an orientation factor in this fixed comparison need not mean
lowering the activation energy.
Likewise, increasing temperature changes the energy distribution and can also
affect collision frequency.
The factor multiplication here uses the stated conditional orientation
fraction
among energetic encounters, so no extra assumption that the two properties are
statistically independent is needed.
This simple model is not a universal quantitative description of every
solution
or surface reaction.
A straight concentration versus time line is not permission to predict
negative
material.
Consider a stipulated zero order disappearance with initial concentration zero
point zero eight molar and a constant loss rate of zero point zero zero two
molar per second.
The line reaches zero at forty seconds.
In an ideal model that maintains this rate until depletion and has no other
source of A, there is no A left between forty and sixty seconds.
A feed pulse is applied at sixty seconds.
It establishes concentration zero point zero four molar, with negligible
volume
change.
If the same zero order regime resumes immediately, ten more seconds remove
zero
point zero two molar, leaving zero point zero two molar at seventy seconds.
Applying the original line continuously through the pause and pulse would lose
both the depletion boundary and the added material.
Real zero order behaviour may fail before complete depletion, so the abrupt
stop and restart are explicit assumptions of this exercise.
Specify each interval and its starting concentration before using the
integrated equation.
A total signal can combine two independent contributions even when each
follows
a simple first order law.
In a supporting model, let two noninterconverting populations contribute
equally to the initial calibrated signal.
One population has a ten minute half life and the other a twenty minute half
life.
Assume signal is linear in their remaining amounts with the stated equal
initial weights and that neither product contributes.
After twenty minutes, the fast population retains one quarter and the slow
population one half.
Their weighted sum is three eighths of the initial signal.
After forty minutes, the corresponding fractions are one sixteenth and one
quarter, giving a total fraction of five divided by thirty two.
The signal ratio from twenty to forty minutes is therefore five twelfths, not
the same multiplier as in the first twenty minute interval.
The total is a sum of exponentials, not generally one exponential with an
averaged half life.
The surviving signal becomes increasingly dominated by the slower population.
A curved logarithmic plot can flag a failed single population model, but it
does not by itself uniquely prove this particular two component explanation.
